original_question: Does there exist a metrizable topological group G that is o-bounded, meaning that for every sequence (U_n) of neighborhoods of the identity there is a sequence (F_n) of finite subsets of G such that G is contained in the union of the sets F_n U_n, and for which Player I nevertheless has a winning strategy in the game OF(G)? In this game, at each stage n, Player I chooses a neighborhood U_n of the identity and Player II chooses a finite subset F_n of G; Player II wins exactly when G is contained in the union of the sets F_n U_n.
target_in_paper: Problem 11 (Banakh) in the unsectioned list of open problems.
correct_elements: Your draft correctly captures the mathematical core of Problem 11: the notion of an o-bounded topological group, the Open-Finite game OF(G), the inning-by-inning choices of neighborhoods and finite sets, and the question whether o-boundedness can still coexist with a winning strategy for Player I.
missing_details: The paper states the problem as 'Is there a (metrizable) o-bounded topological group G ... ?' so metrizability is presented as an optional strengthening, not as a mandatory hypothesis.
Immediately before Problem 11, the paper defines o-boundedness and OF(A) first for an arbitrary subset A of a topological group G, and only then specializes to the case A = G.

The paper's notation uses neighborhoods of the origin of G and the covering condition A ⊂ ⋃_{n∈ω} F_n U_n; your draft uses the equivalent identity-language, but the subset-based formulation is part of the nearby setup.

The nearby context explicitly notes that if G is not o-bounded, then Player I has a winning strategy in OF(G); this explains why the problem is specifically asking whether Player I can still win despite o-boundedness.

The paper also records a contextual restriction: any such example, if it exists, cannot be analytic and abelian, more generally cannot be a SIN-group. This is not part of the hypothesis, but it is part of the immediate problem context.
refined_question: Does there exist an o-bounded topological group G—and even a metrizable one—such that Player I has a winning strategy in the Open-Finite game OF(G)? Here, G is called o-bounded if for every sequence (U_n)_{n∈ω} of neighborhoods of the identity (equivalently, of the origin) there exist finite sets F_n ⊂ G such that G ⊂ ⋃_{n∈ω} F_n U_n; in OF(G), at inning n, Player I chooses such a neighborhood U_n and Player II chooses a finite set F_n ⊂ G, and Player II wins exactly when G ⊂ ⋃_{n∈ω} F_n U_n.
justification: The draft is essentially an expanded restatement of Problem 11 (Banakh). The only substantive paper-faithfulness issue is that the official formulation asks for the existence of such a group with '(metrizable)' in parentheses, rather than requiring metrizability outright. The paragraph immediately preceding Problem 11 supplies the exact definitions of o-boundedness and OF(A), and the sentence immediately after Problem 11 gives the obstruction that any such group cannot be analytic abelian, more generally a SIN-group.
